newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina hopes to set up bond clearing system.
newsitem.headline: Argentina hopes to set up bond clearing system.

text.p: Argentine authorities and banks say they hope to introduce a centralized clearing system for the local bond market in the first quarter of next year in a major move to modernize the country's capital markets.
After setbacks because of the market turmoil last year caused by fallout from the Mexican peso devaluation, an extra push to set up a clearing system for bonds is underway.

The thrust of the plan is coming from Argenclear, a recently established organization that hopes to clear and settle all corporate and government bonds in Argentina through a delivery versus payment system.
Eduardo Trucco, president of Argenclear and head of treasury at Banco Rio de La Plata, one of Argentina's largest banks, told Reuters the system should be ready in the first quarter of next year.

A well-functioning local clearing system for bonds would reduce the risk associated with investing in an emerging market like Argentina and therefore could help attract more foreign investment in domestic instruments.
"To settle with a guarantee would be an advantage to everybody," said the chief trader at a large Argentine bank.

Otherwise, as is the case now, foreign investors may well continue to concentrate their investments in overseas instruments like Argentina's Brady bonds, the bulk of which are traded in New York and London.

Brady bonds are cleared through Euroclear, an international clearing organisation founded in 1968, which provides clearing and settlement and borrowing and lending of securities through a computerised book entry system.
"The idea is to create something like Euroclear in Argentina," said the head trader.
"A clearing system will allow for effective delivery versus payment which will make local trades safer for foreign investors," said Trucco.
The Argentine Economy Ministry has said it wants to gradually replace its foreign currency debt with more domestic issues, making it more important to modernize the local market.

Mario Schiavina, manager of market-making at Argentina's financial watchdog the Comision Nacional de Valores, says one of the requirements of the private pension funds when they were set up in August 1994 was that they could only invest in instruments that could be settled.
The Commission has only granted them temporary authorization to trade in uncleared instruments, making it even more important to swiftly introduce a clearing system.
The lack of a centralized clearing system is partly a function of the the fact that Argentine debt instruments are not all traded in one place.

The domestic Mercado Abierto Electronico (MAE), an electronic over-the-counter market, where trades are registered, accounts for between 60 and 70 percent of the trade, but bonds can also be traded on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange.

Trucco says Argenclear will clear and settle trades from both the MAE and the Stock Exchange. In addition, Argenclear hopes to absorb the operations of the Central Bank's Central de Registracion y Liquidacion (CRYL). The CRYL would act as a depository bank for players in the debt markets.

Stocks are currently cleared and settled through the Mercado de Valores (MerVal) and Trucco said Argenclear could offer one centralized system for clearing and settlement of the guaranteed operations in the MerVal and the non-guaranteed operations in the MAE. That could happen if the MerVal takes a stake in Argenclear and Argenclear oustources its services to the MerVal.
